summaries.example: Imagine you say, “The library is open.” If the library really is open, your statement matches the way things are. A correspondence theory calls this kind of match truth. Another person might ask whether your statement fits with many other things you know, or whether it helps inquiry move toward a settled answer.
summaries.summary: Truth is a central question in philosophy. Philosophers ask what truths are and what, if anything, makes them true. The entry introduces several important approaches. The correspondence theory says that a true belief or statement connects correctly with the world, often through facts. The coherence theory says that truth is connected with belonging to a well-connected system of beliefs. Pragmatist theories link truth with inquiry, experience, and what would remain settled after extended investigation. Later discussions consider how truth can be studied using language, including ideas about sentences, reference, and meaning. Some deflationary views say that “true” does not name a large, deep property and can work mainly as a useful language tool.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask what truth is and what makes something true.
Correspondence theories connect truth with the world.
Coherence theories connect truth with how beliefs fit together.
Pragmatist theories connect truth with inquiry and experience.
There is more than one philosophical answer, and the answers can have different assumptions.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use ideas about truth when we decide whether to trust a report, check a claim, or change our minds. Learning different theories helps us notice that people may disagree not only about an answer, but also about what makes an answer true. It encourages careful checking and respectful questioning.

important_terms.definition: A statement, belief, or sentence that can be true or false because it has meaning.
The idea that something is true when it matches the way the world is.
The idea that a belief is true when it fits well with a connected, consistent system of beliefs.
A family of views connecting truth with useful inquiry, experience, or what would become settled after careful investigation.
The idea that truth may not be a deep thing in the world; saying “it is true that...” can sometimes be another way of saying the statement itself.

questions_to_think_about: Is a statement true because it matches the world, because it fits other beliefs, or for another reason?
Can a belief fit with many other beliefs and still be wrong?
What makes careful inquiry a good way to look for truth?

summaries.example: Suppose a student claims, “The experiment produced gas.” A correspondence theorist asks whether the claim matches what happened in the experiment. A coherence theorist asks how it fits with the student’s other observations and beliefs. A pragmatist may emphasize whether careful, continued inquiry would settle the claim and whether the belief survives later experience. A deflationist may focus on the practical role of saying, “It is true that the experiment produced gas,” rather than treating truth as a substantial property.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of truth asks both what truths are and what makes them true. The entry surveys several major approaches rather than presenting one settled answer. Correspondence theories treat truth as a world-directed relation: a meaningful claim is true when reality contains what is required for it to be correct. Some versions use facts and structured propositions; others try to explain correspondence through reference, satisfaction, and representation without committing to a particular ontology. Coherence theories instead connect truth with a sufficiently coherent system of beliefs, often alongside idealist assumptions. Pragmatist theories emphasize inquiry, experience, verification, and the prospect that a belief would remain settled after sustained investigation. Tarski’s formal theory shows how truth for an interpreted language can be characterized recursively and related to reference and satisfaction, but its formal machinery is compatible with different philosophical interpretations. Realism often links truth with an objective world and bivalence, whereas anti-realism may identify truth with verifiability or warranted assertibility and reject bivalence in some cases. Deflationism denies that truth has a substantial metaphysical nature, emphasizing equivalence, disquotation, or logical usefulness. Truth also connects with meaning, truth conditions, the role of assertion, and pluralist views according to which truth may be realized differently in different domains.
key_ideas: The central problem is to explain what truths are and what makes them true; whether this is a metaphysical problem is itself disputed.
Neo-classical correspondence, coherence, and pragmatist theories make truth part of broader metaphysical or epistemological pictures.
A correspondence theory may appeal to facts and structured propositions, or may instead build truth from reference, satisfaction, and representation without a specific metaphysics of facts.

Tarski’s work provides formal tools for defining truth for interpreted languages through recursive clauses and truth biconditionals, but those tools alone do not settle whether truth is realist or anti-realist.
Realism commonly connects truth with an objective world and bivalence; anti-realism may connect truth with verification or warranted assertibility.
Deflationary theories deny that truth carries substantial metaphysical content, while pluralist theories allow truth to be realized in different ways in different domains.
summaries.why_it_matters: Theories of truth influence how we understand evidence, language, objectivity, and disagreement. They help distinguish a dispute about whether a claim is correct from a deeper dispute about what correctness consists in. The topic also shows why formal work on language, such as Tarski’s, can be philosophically useful without by itself deciding between realism, anti-realism, correspondence, coherence, or deflationism.

important_terms.definition: A meaningful sentence, proposition, belief, or utterance treated as something that can be true or false.
A theory that explains truth through a suitable relation between meaningful content and the world, often involving facts or representation.
A theory that explains truth through membership in, or support from, a sufficiently coherent system of beliefs or judgments.
A family of theories connecting truth with inquiry, experience, verification, or what would remain settled at the end of prolonged investigation.
The view that truth has no substantial metaphysical nature; some versions treat truth-talk as eliminable or mainly as a linguistic and logical device.
The semantic relation by which a term is connected with what it stands for.
A semantic relation between a predicate and the objects that satisfy it, used in Tarskian accounts of truth.
The principle that every truth-bearer is either true or false; anti-realist theories often question this principle.

questions_to_think_about: Does a theory that explains truth through reference and satisfaction genuinely provide correspondence, or does it need a further account of those relations?
Can a belief system be highly coherent while failing to match the world?
Should every meaningful claim be either true or false? What would an anti-realist say about claims that cannot be verified?
Does using the word “true” add content, or can it sometimes function mainly as a useful logical device?
Could different kinds of claims have truth realized in different ways?

summaries.example: A class is trying to decide whether a new playground rule is fair. One student says the rule is true or correct because it describes what the school actually decided. Another says it is correct only if it fits with the class’s other rules and ideas about fairness. A third says the best rule is the one that survives careful discussion and experience. These answers resemble different approaches to truth, although deciding whether a rule is fair can involve issues beyond the theories in the entry.
summaries.summary: Truth is one of philosophy’s broadest subjects because many questions about knowledge, language, and reality depend on it. The basic problem is simple to state: what are truths, and what makes them true? The entry surveys three important neo-classical approaches. Correspondence theory treats truth as a relation between a meaningful claim and the world. In one influential version, a proposition corresponds to a fact when their structures and parts match. Coherence theory instead explains truth through a claim’s place in a suitably coherent system of beliefs. Pragmatist theories connect truth with inquiry and experience: Peirce is associated with truth as the eventual result of inquiry, while James connects truth with what is satisfactory to believe and with future experience. Tarski’s work gives a formal account of truth for interpreted languages. Through recursive definitions, reference, and satisfaction, it shows how the truth of complex sentences can be built from simpler parts. Yet this formal apparatus can be used by realist and anti-realist theories alike. Realism emphasizes an objective world and often bivalence. Anti-realism may identify truth with verification or warranted assertibility and question bivalence. Deflationism takes a more modest view, arguing that truth may not be a substantial property and that truth language can help us make general or otherwise difficult claims. The entry also examines truth’s connections with meaning, truth conditions, assertion, and pluralism.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about both the nature of truth and whether truth needs a deep metaphysical explanation.
Correspondence theories look from language or thought toward the world; coherence theories look at relations among beliefs.
Pragmatist theories emphasize inquiry and the way beliefs respond to experience.
Tarski’s approach gives formal methods for handling truth in interpreted languages, but it does not by itself choose between realist and anti-realist interpretations.
Realists generally treat the world as objective and independent of our descriptions; anti-realists may make truth depend more closely on verification or warranted assertion.
Deflationists argue that truth-talk may be less mysterious and less metaphysically important than other theories suggest.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about truth improves how we evaluate claims and understand disagreements. It reveals that a debate can concern evidence, the structure of beliefs, the nature of reality, or the purpose of the word “true.” These distinctions matter in science, everyday reasoning, and discussions about how language represents the world.

important_terms.definition: Something meaningful, such as a sentence or belief, that can be evaluated as true or false.
The view that a claim is true when it correctly matches the way things are in the world.
The view that a claim is true when it belongs to a connected and sufficiently consistent system of beliefs.
A view that relates truth to inquiry, experience, verification, or what careful investigation would eventually settle.
A group of theories saying that truth does not have a large, independent metaphysical nature and may mainly serve a language or logic function.
The connection between a word or expression and what it stands for.
The relation by which an object meets the condition expressed by a predicate.
The idea that every truth-bearer must be either true or false.

questions_to_think_about: If a belief fits with many other beliefs, does that guarantee that it matches reality?
Can truth be connected with successful inquiry without simply meaning “whatever is useful”?
Why might a formal theory of truth leave philosophical questions unanswered?
What kinds of claims might create difficulty for the principle of bivalence?
Is “That is true” sometimes useful even when it seems to repeat an earlier statement?
